meta.provenance: Authored from model knowledge (cutoff Jan 2026). Original explanations. Node names/categories are factual data.

commands.name: Number Slider
commands.description: An interactive slider that outputs a number within a set range and step. Wire it into dimensions, counts or rotation angles so you can drag through design variations and watch the model respond live.

commands.name: Integer Slider
commands.description: A slider constrained to whole numbers, ideal for counts — panels in a facade, treads in a stair, items in a range. Use it instead of Number Slider wherever fractional values would break the logic downstream.

commands.name: Number
commands.description: A simple box holding a fixed numeric value. Use it for constants you want visible and labelled on the canvas rather than buried inside a code block.

commands.name: Boolean
commands.description: A true/false toggle used to switch logic branches, flip conditions or gate parts of a graph. Pair it with If to give a script simple on/off behaviour a non-programmer can operate.

commands.name: String
commands.description: A text input box outputting whatever is typed into it. The usual source for parameter names, prefixes and search terms that the rest of the graph consumes.

commands.name: Code Block
commands.description: A freeform node where DesignScript is typed directly — numbers, strings, ranges like 0..10..2, functions and multi-line expressions. Experienced users compress whole clusters of nodes into one tidy code block; double-click empty canvas to create one.

commands.name: File Path
commands.description: Opens a file browser and outputs the chosen file's path as a string. The standard front door for graphs that read Excel, images or text files.

commands.name: Directory Path
commands.description: Outputs the path of a chosen folder, for graphs that batch through many files or need somewhere to write exports. Combine with file-listing logic to process a whole directory of drawings or spreadsheets.

commands.name: File.FromPath
commands.description: Converts a path string into a file object that reading nodes can consume. A small but necessary adaptor between File Path and nodes like File.ReadText.

commands.name: Number Range
commands.description: Generates a list of numbers from a start to an end value at a given step — the graph equivalent of 0..100..5. The seed of most repetitive geometry: point grids, panel setout, level elevations.

commands.name: Number Sequence
commands.description: Generates a list by count rather than end value — start, amount and step. Use it when you know how many items you need, such as one value per panel or per level.

commands.name: Object.IsNull
commands.description: Returns true for null items in a list, which is the first step in cleaning data that came back patchy from Revit or Excel. Feed the result into List.FilterByBoolMask to strip the nulls out.

commands.name: Watch
commands.description: Displays the data flowing through a wire — values, list structure, nesting depth. The single most important debugging habit in Dynamo: watch early, watch often, and list-structure surprises get caught before they multiply.

commands.name: Watch 3D
commands.description: A miniature 3D viewport showing only the geometry wired into it, independent of the main background preview. Useful for isolating one branch of geometry in a busy graph.

commands.name: Watch Image
commands.description: Previews an image object on the canvas, for graphs that read bitmaps — heightmap-driven facades, image-sampled colour studies. Confirms the right picture is loaded before pixel values drive anything.

commands.name: Color.ByARGB
commands.description: Builds a colour from alpha, red, green and blue values. Feed it into display or override nodes to colour-code geometry by analysis results — area, deviation, parameter values.

commands.name: Display.ByGeometryColor
commands.description: Draws geometry in the preview tinted with a supplied colour, without touching Revit. The standard way to build in-canvas heat maps — remap a value to a colour range and see the gradient across your geometry.

commands.name: Python Script
commands.description: Embeds a Python node with access to the full Revit API, for logic that stock nodes cannot express — transactions, element filters, edge cases. The escape hatch when visual programming runs out of road; keep inputs and outputs clearly named.

commands.name: Note
commands.description: Places a free text note on the canvas explaining what a section of the graph does. Graphs are read far more often than written — a few notes turn a private puzzle into a tool colleagues can trust.

commands.name: Group
commands.description: Wraps selected nodes in a coloured, titled container — inputs, processing, outputs — so the graph reads as a storyboard. Consistent grouping and colour conventions are the mark of a shareable script.

commands.name: Freeze
commands.description: Right-click option that suspends a node and everything downstream of it without deleting anything. Freeze the expensive Revit-writing end of a graph while you iterate safely on the logic upstream.

commands.name: Run (Automatic/Manual)
commands.description: Switches the graph between re-executing on every change and running only when you press Run. Use Manual whenever the graph writes to Revit or does heavy geometry — Automatic is for lightweight exploratory work.

commands.name: Data.OpenXMLImportExcel
commands.description: Reads a worksheet from an Excel file into nested lists, one list per row, without needing Excel installed. The start of every spreadsheet-to-Revit workflow: room data sheets, door schedules, setting-out tables.

commands.name: Data.OpenXMLExportExcel
commands.description: Writes nested lists out to an Excel worksheet, starting at a given row and column. Pair with parameter-reading nodes to push live model data — areas, counts, door ironmongery — into spreadsheets others can work with.

commands.name: Data.ParseJSON
commands.description: Converts a JSON string into Dynamo dictionaries and lists. Useful for reading configuration files or data handed over from web services and other tools.

commands.name: File.ReadText
commands.description: Reads a text file into a single string, ready for splitting into lines and fields. The simple route for CSVs and logs when full Excel handling is overkill.

commands.name: Passthrough
commands.description: Passes its first input straight through, but only after its second input has arrived — a way to force execution order. Essential when one Revit operation must finish before another starts, which Dynamo's dataflow cannot otherwise guarantee.

commands.name: FamilyInstance.Room
commands.description: Returns the room each family instance sits in, closing a gap in the native node set. The key to workflows like writing room names onto furniture and equipment parameters for schedules.

commands.name: UI.MultipleInputForm ++
commands.description: Builds a pop-up dialog with text boxes, dropdowns and selectors so end users can run a graph without opening Dynamo. The de facto standard for turning scripts into office tools, especially via Dynamo Player.

commands.name: List.Create
commands.description: Bundles separate inputs into a single list, with a + button to add more ports. Use it to gather results from parallel branches before a node that expects one collection.

commands.name: List.Map
commands.description: Applies a function to every item in a list, returning the transformed list. Largely superseded by lacing and list levels for simple cases, but still the clearest way to run a custom function across a collection.

commands.name: List.Combine
commands.description: Applies a function pairwise across two or more lists — first with firsts, second with seconds. Reach for it when a straightforward wire-up mangles the pairing between corresponding items.

commands.name: List.FilterByBoolMask
commands.description: Splits a list into 'in' and 'out' streams according to a parallel list of true/false values. The workhorse of every selection workflow: build a test, mask the list, keep what passes.

commands.name: List.Sort
commands.description: Orders a list of comparable values — numbers or strings — ascending. Combine with List.Reverse for descending order.

commands.name: List.SortByKey
commands.description: Sorts one list using a parallel list of keys — order rooms by area, sheets by number, points by elevation. The keys travel with the items, so both come back in matching order.

commands.name: List.Flatten
commands.description: Collapses nested lists into a single flat list, optionally by a set number of levels. Use it deliberately — flattening everything is the quick fix that often destroys the structure a later node needed.

commands.name: List.Chop
commands.description: Cuts a flat list into sublists of given lengths — the inverse of flattening. Classic for rebuilding rows from a stream of values, such as turning a point list back into a grid.

commands.name: List.Transpose
commands.description: Swaps rows and columns in a nested list, so a list of rows becomes a list of columns. Indispensable around Excel import and export, where orientation rarely arrives the way you want it.

commands.name: List.GetItemAtIndex
commands.description: Pulls the item at a given position from a list, counting from zero. With a list of indices it extracts several at once — the basic tool for picking a column out of imported spreadsheet rows.

commands.name: List.Count
commands.description: Returns how many items a list contains. A quiet debugging hero: matching counts at both ends of an operation is the quickest sanity check that nothing got dropped.

commands.name: List.Reverse
commands.description: Flips the order of a list end to end. Useful after sorting, or for correcting curve and boundary directions expressed as point lists.

commands.name: List.FirstItem
commands.description: Returns the first item of a list. Commonly used to strip a header row's partner, grab a single test element or peel one sample from a big set while developing.

commands.name: List.LastItem
commands.description: Returns the final item of a list, whatever its length. Handy for end points of point sequences and the newest item of sorted data.

commands.name: List.Contains
commands.description: Tests whether a list includes a given item, returning true or false. Use it to check membership against an approved list — type names, level names — before acting.

commands.name: List.IndexOf
commands.description: Returns the position of an item within a list, or -1 if absent. Pair with List.GetItemAtIndex to look values up across parallel lists, dictionary-style.

commands.name: List.Join
commands.description: Concatenates several lists into one continuous list, preserving order. Unlike List.Create, which nests its inputs, Join splices them end to end.

commands.name: List.UniqueItems
commands.description: Removes duplicates, keeping the first occurrence of each value. The standard first move for building a clean set of type names, materials or levels actually used in a model.

commands.name: List.GroupByKey
commands.description: Buckets items into sublists according to matching keys — rooms grouped by department, walls by type name. Returns both the groups and their unique keys, ready for per-group processing or reporting.

commands.name: List.TakeItems
commands.description: Keeps the first n items of a list (or the last n with a negative count). Useful for sampling a subset while testing, or trimming a list to a known length.

commands.name: List.DropItems
commands.description: Discards the first n items of a list (or the last n with a negative count). The classic way to skip a header row from imported spreadsheet data.

commands.name: List.AddItemToEnd
commands.description: Appends a single item to the end of a list. Small but constant duty in assembling rows for export or closing loops of points.

commands.name: List.IsEmpty
commands.description: Returns true when a list has no items. Wire it into conditional logic so a graph fails gracefully when a selection or filter comes back with nothing.

commands.name: List.Cycle
commands.description: Repeats a list a given number of times end to end. Useful for tiling patterns — alternate panel types, repeated colour sequences — across a longer set of targets.

commands.name: If
commands.description: Chooses between two inputs according to a boolean test — true takes the first, false the second. The basic branching node; combine with comparison nodes to make graphs respond to conditions.

commands.name: And
commands.description: Returns true only when all its boolean inputs are true. Use it to combine tests — right category and right level — before filtering.

commands.name: Or
commands.description: Returns true when any of its boolean inputs is true. The partner to And for building compound conditions.

commands.name: Not
commands.description: Inverts a boolean — true becomes false and vice versa. Often the quickest way to flip a filter, keeping what a test rejected.
Tests whether two values are equal, returning true or false, and laces across lists to test many at once. The seed of most filtering: compare parameter values to a target and mask the results.

commands.name: Math.RemapRange
commands.description: Rescales a list of numbers from their current spread to a new minimum and maximum. The engine behind data-driven design — remap distances to panel openings, areas to colours, anything to anything.

commands.name: Math.Round
commands.description: Rounds a number to the nearest whole value or given number of decimals. Tidy values before writing them into parameters or spreadsheets that humans will read.

commands.name: Math.Floor
commands.description: Rounds a number down to the nearest integer. Useful for working out how many whole units — panels, treads, tiles — fit within a dimension.

commands.name: Math.Ceiling
commands.description: Rounds a number up to the nearest integer. The counterpart to Math.Floor when you need to be sure of covering a dimension rather than fitting inside it.

commands.name: Math.Abs
commands.description: Returns the absolute value of a number, stripping the sign. Common in tolerance checks where only the size of a difference matters, not its direction.

commands.name: Math.Sin
commands.description: Returns the sine of an angle given in degrees. Feed it a number range to generate wave forms for undulating facades, ceilings and screens.

commands.name: Math.Cos
commands.description: Returns the cosine of an angle given in degrees. With Math.Sin it converts angles into x and y components for radial arrays and circular setout.

commands.name: Math.PI
commands.description: Outputs the constant pi. Used in circumference, arc-length and radian conversions inside geometric setout.

commands.name: String.Concat
commands.description: Joins several strings into one, in port order. The standard way to build parameter values like room codes from prefix, number and suffix parts.

commands.name: String.Split
commands.description: Cuts a string into a list wherever a separator occurs — commas for CSV rows, hyphens for door numbers. The first move in parsing any structured text.

commands.name: String.Join
commands.description: Combines a list of strings into one, inserting a separator between each. The inverse of String.Split, used to reassemble codes and to build readable report lines.

commands.name: String.Contains
commands.description: Tests whether a string includes a given fragment, returning true or false. Combined with a filter it finds every type name containing a keyword — all walls with 'EX', all views with 'WIP'.

commands.name: String.Replace
commands.description: Swaps every occurrence of a fragment within a string for new text. The engine of batch renaming workflows — views, sheets, family types — when paired with name-setting nodes.

commands.name: String.ToNumber
commands.description: Parses a string into a numeric value. Necessary after Excel import or text parameters, where numbers often arrive disguised as text and refuse to calculate.

commands.name: String from Object
commands.description: Converts any value — number, element, boolean — into its text representation. Use it before concatenation or export, and for readable debugging output.

commands.name: String.ToUpper
commands.description: Converts a string to upper case. Useful for enforcing drawing-standard capitalisation on names and title text, or normalising values before comparison.

commands.name: Point.ByCoordinates
commands.description: Creates a point from x, y and z values, and with list inputs and lacing settings, whole grids of points at once. The atom of computational geometry — most parametric setout begins here.

commands.name: Point.Origin
commands.description: Outputs the point at 0,0,0. A convenient anchor for base planes, coordinate systems and geometry that will be moved into place later.

commands.name: Vector.ByCoordinates
commands.description: Creates a direction vector from x, y and z components. Vectors carry direction and magnitude for translations, extrusions and normals — they position nothing by themselves.

commands.name: Vector.XAxis
commands.description: Outputs the unit vector along the world x axis. A ready-made direction for offsets, arrays and mirror axes without building a vector by hand.

commands.name: Vector.ZAxis
commands.description: Outputs the unit vector pointing straight up the world z axis. The default direction for vertical extrusions, level offsets and rotation axes in plan.

commands.name: Plane.ByOriginNormal
commands.description: Creates a plane from a point on it and a vector perpendicular to it. Planes serve as mirrors, section cutters and hosts for sketch-like operations throughout the geometry library.

commands.name: Plane.XY
commands.description: Outputs the world ground plane at the origin. The usual base for flat setout and a quick mirror or section plane at level zero.

commands.name: CoordinateSystem.ByOrigin
commands.description: Creates a coordinate system located at a given point, axes aligned to the world. Transform nodes can then move, rotate and scale geometry relative to it rather than the world origin.

commands.name: Line.ByStartPointEndPoint
commands.description: Creates a straight line between two points, and with paired lists, whole families of lines at once. The basic stroke for setout, structure lines and edges that later become walls or beams.

commands.name: Line.ByStartPointDirectionLength
commands.description: Creates a line from a start point, a direction vector and a length. Preferable to two-point construction when the geometry is naturally described as origin plus direction, such as grid rays.

commands.name: Arc.ByThreePoints
commands.description: Fits a circular arc through three points — start, a point on the curve and end. Handy for curved walls and paths defined by survey or setting-out points rather than centre and radius.

commands.name: Circle.ByCenterPointRadius
commands.description: Creates a circle from a centre point and radius, optionally on a given normal. A frequent base curve for radial setout, columns of points and extruded cylinders.

commands.name: Rectangle.ByWidthLength
commands.description: Creates a closed rectangle of given width and length, centred on a plane or coordinate system. A quick closed profile for floor outlines, panel boundaries and extrusion bases.

commands.name: Polygon.ByPoints
commands.description: Connects a list of points into a closed polygon, joining the last point back to the first. Use it for boundary outlines destined to become floors, regions or extrusion profiles.

commands.name: PolyCurve.ByPoints
commands.description: Chains a list of points into a connected polycurve, open or closed. The workhorse for paths and boundaries built from computed point lists, feeding walls, railings and sweeps.

commands.name: NurbsCurve.ByPoints
commands.description: Fits a smooth freeform curve through a list of points. The route to flowing geometry — sinuous walls, sculpted rails — from a handful of control locations.

commands.name: Curve.PointAtParameter
commands.description: Returns the point at a normalised position along a curve, 0 at the start and 1 at the end. Feed it a range of parameters to sprinkle points along any curve for panels, mullions or planting.

commands.name: Curve.PointsAtEqualSegmentLength
commands.description: Divides a curve into segments of equal length and returns the division points. The honest way to space elements evenly along a curve, since equal parameter steps are not equal distances on most curves.

commands.name: Curve.Length
commands.description: Returns the length of a curve in model units. Sums neatly across lists for quick take-offs of skirting runs, kerb lines or duct routes.

commands.name: Curve.Offset
commands.description: Creates a parallel copy of a curve at a set distance, sign controlling the side. Used for wall centrelines to faces, path edges and nested boundary patterns.

commands.name: Curve.Extrude
commands.description: Sweeps a curve along a direction vector to create a surface. The quick way to raise a fence of surfaces from plan curves — walls-to-be, screens, ribbons.

commands.name: Curve.ExtrudeAsSolid
commands.description: Extrudes a closed curve into a solid of given distance. The one-step massing tool: draw a footprint, extrude it, and interrogate volume or intersections immediately.

commands.name: Surface.ByPatch
commands.description: Fills a closed curve with a flat surface, like stretching a skin across a boundary. The standard step between a closed outline and area measurement or solid modelling.

commands.name: Surface.ByLoft
commands.description: Skins a smooth surface through an ordered list of cross-section curves. The primary tool for doubly-curved facades, canopies and terrain-like surfaces from profile families.

commands.name: Surface.PointAtParameter
commands.description: Returns the point at a u,v position on a surface, 0 to 1 in each direction. Cross two ranges and you have a point grid draped over any surface — the seed of panelling workflows.

commands.name: Surface.NormalAtParameter
commands.description: Returns the vector perpendicular to a surface at a u,v position. Essential for orienting panels and components so they sit flush on curved surfaces rather than all facing one way.

commands.name: Surface.Thicken
commands.description: Gives a surface physical depth, producing a solid, optionally thickened both sides. The usual last step before turning abstract skins into wall-like or slab-like solids for import or clash checks.

commands.name: Surface.Area
commands.description: Returns the area of a surface in model units. Combined with patching room or facade boundaries, it powers quick comparative area studies outside the Revit schedule system.

commands.name: Cuboid.ByLengths
commands.description: Creates a box solid of given width, length and height about an origin. The quickest test solid for massing studies, clash proxies and bounding volumes.

commands.name: Sphere.ByCenterPointRadius
commands.description: Creates a sphere solid from a centre and radius. Often used as a visual marker at key points or as a soft proxy for clearance zones around equipment.

commands.name: Solid.Union
commands.description: Fuses two or more solids into one. Use it to consolidate massing pieces before measuring volume or exporting a single clean object.

commands.name: Solid.Difference
commands.description: Subtracts one solid from another, carving openings, courtyards and cuts. With massing solids it answers questions like how much volume remains after removing circulation.

commands.name: Geometry.Translate
commands.description: Moves geometry by a vector or by x, y, z distances, returning a moved copy. With lists and lacing it becomes an array engine — one profile stepped along a range makes a whole set.

commands.name: Geometry.Rotate
commands.description: Rotates geometry about an origin and axis by an angle in degrees. Feed it a list of angles for radial arrays and twisting stacked-floor studies.

commands.name: Geometry.Scale
commands.description: Scales geometry uniformly or per axis about a base point. Useful for unit fixes on imported geometry and for graded families of shapes in pattern studies.

commands.name: Geometry.Mirror
commands.description: Reflects geometry about a plane, returning the mirrored copy. Use world planes for quick handing or a constructed plane for arbitrary mirror lines.

commands.name: Geometry.Intersect
commands.description: Returns the shared geometry where two inputs overlap — a plane through a solid yields section curves, two solids yield their common volume. A core analytical tool for slicing and overlap studies.

commands.name: Geometry.Split
commands.description: Cuts geometry into pieces using another piece of geometry as the knife — a plane through a solid, a curve across a surface. Returns all fragments for you to keep or discard.

commands.name: Geometry.Trim
commands.description: Splits geometry with a cutting tool and discards the side nearest a picked point, keeping the rest. The tidy alternative to Split when you already know which portion should survive.

commands.name: Geometry.DistanceTo
commands.description: Measures the shortest distance between two pieces of geometry. Across lists it builds proximity fields — distance from each panel to an attractor point — that drive data-responsive designs.

commands.name: Geometry.DoesIntersect
commands.description: Returns true if two pieces of geometry touch or overlap. A lightweight clash and containment test — which desks fall inside a zone, which pipes cross a wall.

commands.name: Geometry.BoundingBox
commands.description: Returns the axis-aligned box that just encloses geometry. Useful for overall sizes, spatial sorting and generating simplified proxies for heavy elements.
